7 Microorganisms in the environment

7.1 Microorganisms

Key words: agar jelly · algae · bacteria · colony · fungi · microorganism · mushroom · Petri dish · protozoa · single-celled · sterile · toadstool · yeast

What is a microorganism?

A microorganism is a living organism that is so small that you can only see it clearly by using a microscope.

Like all living organisms, microorganisms are made of cells. Many microorganisms are made of only one cell — they are single-celled.

There are several different kinds of microorganism:

KindWhat it is like
bacteriasingle-celled; much smaller than animal or plant cells
microscopic fungisome are single cells (yeast), some are tangles of very thin threads
protozoaanimal-like microorganisms, common in pond water
algaeplant-like microorganisms, common in pond water

Bacteria

Bacteria are everywhere. (Bacteria is a plural word. The singular word, for just one of them, is bacterium.)

Each bacterium is made of a single cell. Cells of bacteria are much smaller than animal cells or plant cells. You could fit 1000 bacteria, lined up end to end, between two of the millimetre marks on your ruler.

Most bacteria are harmless, but there are a few kinds that can make you ill.

Fungi

Fungi (singular: fungus) are not always microorganisms. Many fungi, including mushrooms and toadstools, are large and easy to see.

But be careful with what a mushroom actually is:

  • A mushroom or toadstool is only part of the fungus's body, and it only grows at certain times of year.
  • Most of the time the fungus is just a tangle of very thin threads, often growing under the ground or inside a dead log. Those threads are so thin that they are difficult to see without a microscope.
  • Some kinds of fungi never produce mushrooms or toadstools at all. They are made of single cells, not threads, so they are definitely microorganisms.

Yeast is one of these. The powdery white substance you sometimes see on the surface of grapes is made up of millions of yeast cells. Yeast is a microscopic, single-celled fungus, and it feeds on the sugar in the grapes.

Yeast reproduces by growing little buds out of its cells. You can see the buds if you look closely through a microscope.

Growing microorganisms

A single microorganism is too small to see without a microscope. But when it is left to grow, a single cell of a bacterium or a fungus divides repeatedly to make a collection of many cells. This collection of cells is called a colony, and a colony is big enough to see without a microscope.

Scientists grow microorganisms safely in the laboratory in a Petri dish containing a special kind of jelly called agar jelly.

The dish and the jelly have to be sterile. Sterile means that any living organisms on them have been killed. If the dish were not sterile, you would not know whether the colonies that grew came from the air or were already there.

Microscopic algae and protozoa

If you look at some pond water through a microscope, you will see many tiny living organisms in the water:

  • Some are tiny plant-like organisms, called algae (singular: alga). Their cells have cell walls and green colouring inside them.
  • Some are animal-like organisms, called protozoa (singular: protozoan). Their cells have no cell wall and no green colouring.

Not all of them are single-celled. Some have cells arranged end to end in long threads, and some are arranged in a sphere.

Questions from the book — 7.1
  1. Viruses are even smaller than bacteria. Suggest why they are not usually said to be microorganisms. Viruses are not generally considered to be living organisms. They show none of the characteristics of living organisms apart from reproduction, and they can only do that inside a cell.
  2. We can see yeast on the surface of fruit. Why is yeast classed as a microorganism? What we see on the fruit is a very large number of individual cells — a colony. Each individual cell is a complete organism, and a single cell can only be seen with a microscope.
  3. Some of the microorganisms in the photograph are not single-celled. How are their cells arranged? The cells are arranged end to end in long threads. Some are also arranged in a sphere.
  4. Drawing microorganisms with plant-like and animal-like cells. a Draw one or two of the bluish-white cells (animal-like). b Draw one of the cells or threads with green colouring (plant-like). c The labels should show that the plant-like cells have cell walls and green colouring inside them (chlorophyll — the chloroplasts themselves are not visible). Animal cells do not have these features.
Think like a scientist — growing microorganisms from the air

You leave the lid off a sterile Petri dish of sterile agar jelly, then tape it shut and leave it to grow.

  1. What are nutrients? Nutrients are materials that organisms need for growth and to provide energy.
  2. Why must the dish and jelly be sterile? The purpose of the investigation is to grow microorganisms that have come from the air. You do not want to grow any microorganisms that were on the dish before you took the lid off.
  3. Drawings of what grew. These will depend on what has grown on your agar jelly.
Workbook — Exercise 7.1 Microorganisms experiment
  1. Reading the results. Read the number of colonies from each dish in the diagram.
  2. Which variables were kept the same? The length of time he leaves the lid off, and the type of jelly in the dish.
  3. Conclusion about the two classrooms. There are more microorganisms in the air in Classroom 203 than in Classroom 204.
  4. Conclusion about temperature. Bacteria grow faster at a temperature of 30 °C than at 10 °C.
  5. Plan an experiment on temperature and bacterial growth. Set up at least three Petri dishes with agar jelly exactly as before. Put all three in the same place and take off the lids for exactly the same time. Then put one in a cold place (a fridge), one in the laboratory at room temperature and one in a warmer place (an incubator), measuring each temperature with a thermometer. Leave the dishes for a set time and measure the sizes of the colonies in each dish — or measure them each day for several days. Keep the other variables the same, for example how long the agar is exposed. If the hypothesis is correct, the colonies in the warm dishes will be larger than those in the cold dishes.

7.2 Food chains and webs

Key words: carnivore · consumer · ecology · food chain · food web · herbivore · predator · prey · producer

Microorganisms in the environment

The study of organisms in their environment is called ecology. All the different organisms that live together affect one another in some way — one species of animal may eat another, or a plant may provide shelter for an animal.

Microorganisms have important roles to play in the environment. In this topic you will look at how food chains and food webs describe how energy, in the form of food, is transferred between plants and animals. In the next topics you will see how microorganisms fit into them.

Food chains

The energy in food begins in the Sun.

  1. Energy from the Sun reaches the Earth in sunlight.
  2. Plants use the energy in sunlight to make their own food. Some of that energy goes into the food the plant stores in its roots, stems, fruits and leaves.
  3. When an animal eats part of the plant, it eats the food the plant made, and that is how the animal gets its energy.

Passing energy on like this is called energy transfer, and you show it by drawing a food chain. The arrows in a food chain show the direction in which the energy is passed on.

Every organism in a food chain has a name for its role:

TermWhat it means
producerthe first organism in the chain — a plant, which uses energy from the Sun to produce food
consumerevery other organism in the chain; animals are always consumers, because they must eat ready-made food
herbivorea consumer that eats only plants
carnivorea consumer that eats other animals
predatoran animal that catches, kills and eats other animals
preythe animals that a predator eats

Food webs

Here are two food chains from the African plains:

  • acacia tree → springbok → cheetah
  • grass → termite → aardvark → leopard

In real life the same organisms appear in several food chains at once. A diagram that joins them all up is a food web.

To trace a food chain inside a food web, put your finger on a producer and follow the arrows: acacia tree → springbok → cheetah. Then try another, starting at the grass and ending at the leopard.

In this food web:

  • The producers are the acacia tree and the grass.
  • There are 7 consumers.
  • There are 3 herbivores (springbok, zebra and termite).
  • The carnivores are the cheetah, leopard, hyena and aardvark.
  • Predator–prey pairs include cheetah and springbok, leopard and hyena, aardvark and termites, hyena and springbok.

A food chain or food web is a model. It is useful because it shows the feeding relationships in a simple, visual way. But it is not perfect: many more organisms would really be part of the web, and the diagram does not tell you how important each relationship is — for example, whether leopards eat mostly hyenas or mostly zebras.

Questions from the book — 7.2
  1. The chicken Arun ate had eaten wheat. Draw the food chain. Sunlight → wheat → chicken → Arun, with an arrow at each step.
  2. Draw a food chain for something you ate. This depends on your choice of food, but it must begin with the Sun and a plant.
  3. Write down two more food chains from the food web. Accept any food chain that can be traced along the arrows of the food web.
  4. Name the two producers. Acacia tree and grass.
  5. How many consumers are there? 7.
  6. How many herbivores are there? 3.
  7. Name two carnivores. Any two from cheetah, leopard, hyena and aardvark.
  8. Name two predators and their prey. Any two from: cheetah (predator) and springbok, zebra or aardvark (prey); leopard (predator) and hyena, springbok, zebra or aardvark (prey); aardvark (predator) and termites (prey); hyena (predator) and springbok (prey).
Think like a scientist — using a food web as a model

How well does the African food web show what really happens? A food web is useful because it shows the feeding relationships between organisms in a simple and visual way, and you can see how energy passes from one organism to another. It is far from a complete picture, though: in reality many more organisms are part of the web, and the model does not tell you how important each feeding relationship is.

7.3 Microorganisms and decay

Key words: decay · decomposer · mould · organic matter · rot

Decomposers and decay

The food chains and food webs in the last topic did not include microorganisms. But microorganisms are everywhere — in the air, in the soil, in water, on our skin and inside our bodies.

Look at a mouldy apple. Each spot on the apple is a colony made up of millions of cells of microscopic fungi. This kind of fungus is often called mould, and the apple is said to be mouldy.

The microorganisms have changed the apple — they have made it decay. Organisms that make things decay are called decomposers. Many different kinds of microorganism are decomposers, including some kinds of bacteria and some microscopic fungi.

Apples come from plants, which are living organisms. Any substance that has been made by a living organism — by a plant or an animal — is called organic matter. So an apple is organic matter.

Some microorganisms can break down organic matter when they feed on it. That is what has happened to the apple: the microscopic fungi have broken down the crisp, fresh apple and made it brown and soft. They have made it rot.

Things made of organic matter — bread, leather, wood, fruit — can be broken down by microorganisms. Things that are not organic matter — water, rock, glass, metal, plastic — cannot.

Questions from the book — 7.3
  1. Some microorganisms are decomposers. Explain what this means. Decomposers break down organic material, making it decay.
  2. Describe one way in which decay by microorganisms is not useful. For example, they make food go bad.
  3. Suggest one way in which decay by microorganisms is useful. For example, they change food from one form into another, such as milk into yoghurt; or they get rid of dead bodies and waste material.
Activity 7.3.1 — what can microorganisms decay?
  1. Which of these are made of organic matter? bread · water · leather · rock · wood · fruit Bread, leather, wood and fruit.
  2. Two more of each. Any two more things made of organic matter, and any two things that are not.
  3. Which can be broken down by microorganisms? Bread, leather, wood, fruit, and the two organic items you named.
Think like a scientist — temperature, moisture and decay

Temperature. Two similar pieces of moist bread are kept in different places and watched each day.

  1. Results. The bread goes mouldy more quickly in the warm place than in the fridge. If you collect quantitative results you can make a quantitative comparison.
  2. Differences between groups. These could come from using different bread, covering it differently, making the bread wetter, or how many microorganisms fell onto the bread while it was exposed to the air.
  3. Conclusion. Higher temperatures speed up decay by microorganisms.

Moisture. Plan an experiment to test the hypothesis moist bread decays more quickly than dry bread. The plan should say that the amount of water will be varied and how; how decay will be measured, for example by estimating the area of bread covered by mould; which variables are kept the same (temperature, type of bread, time exposed to the air, type of covering); and a prediction — that decay will be faster on moist bread.

Workbook — Exercises 7.3A, 7.3B and 7.3C

Exercise 7.3A Decomposers in a compost heap. 1 Circle the glass, metal and plastic. 2 These things are not organic and cannot be broken down by microorganisms. 3 To show that microorganisms are present, mix the material with water, spread a little of the mixture onto sterile agar jelly in a Petri dish and leave it for some days; microorganisms will form colonies on the agar. A second dish with only water added is a useful control.

Exercise 7.3B Investigating leaf decay. 1 The greatest loss is the October result for the leaves in the 1 cm mesh bag. 2 The bag with the 1 cm mesh. 3 Microorganisms, earthworms and other small animals. 4 Parts of the leaves disappeared because they decayed; decay was greatest when earthworms and other small animals, as well as microorganisms, could reach the leaves.

Exercise 7.3C Analysing data about mould on bread. 1 Place a mesh, or transparent paper marked in squares of known size, over the mould and count the squares it covers. 2 Circle the value 5 for bread sample 2 in dish 4 (the anomalous result). 3 Mean = 16 mm² (strictly 16.0 mm², to match the other means). 4 Mean = 11.7 mm². 6 Variables the girls could not control include differences in moisture, the number of mould spores landing on each piece, small differences in nutrients in the bread, and the difficulty of estimating an irregular area. 7 A good conclusion: mould grows best on bread at about 40 °C; growth increases as temperature increases up to 40 °C, and falls again above it.

7.4 Microorganisms in food webs

Key words: dung · nutrients

Roles of decomposers

No-one would want to eat a rotten apple — there, the microorganisms have spoiled the food.

But most of the time decay is useful. Microorganisms break down dead bodies and animal waste; they decompose this material. Almost all decomposers are microorganisms, and fungi and bacteria are the most important decomposers.

Two reasons decomposers matter:

  • If dead bodies and waste were not broken down they would simply build up — there would be heaps of dead plants, dead animals and animal dung everywhere.
  • More importantly, dead bodies and waste contain substances that living organisms need for energy and growth. These substances are called nutrients. When microorganisms decay organic matter they return the nutrients to the soil, where plants can use them to grow. That helps animals too, because there are then more plants to eat.

Decomposers in food webs

Decomposers feed on almost every organism after it dies, and on waste from animals. That is how decay microorganisms get their energy: energy from the dead organisms and their waste is transferred to the decomposers.

You can show this by adding decomposers to a food chain or food web. It is not usually done, because you have to draw an arrow from every organism to the decomposers, which makes the diagram look very complicated.

Decomposers are consumers, not producers — they do not make their own food.

DDT in food webs

DDT is a chemical used to kill the mosquitoes that transmit malaria. In many countries where malaria is present, DDT is sprayed inside houses; it sticks to the walls, keeps working for up to six months, and needs much less DDT than spraying outdoors.

DDT is persistent — it lasts for a long time. If DDT gets into a lake or river, more than half of it will still be there 150 years later. That is why DDT turns up in animals far from where it was used, such as albatrosses on Midway Atoll.

DDT in birds of prey makes the shells of their eggs very thin, so the eggs break before the young birds hatch. In the USA, numbers of bald eagles fell while DDT was used. DDT was banned in 1972, and the number of young raised then rose again.

Malaria is still a very large problem: in 2015 there were 212 million cases and 429 000 deaths; in 2016 there were 216 million cases and 445 000 deaths. More than two-thirds of those who die from malaria are children under the age of 5. DDT has been completely banned in 34 countries, but many countries — including India and many African countries — still use it.

Questions from the book — 7.4
  1. Write a food chain of your own and add decomposers to it. The food chain should begin with a producer, with arrows pointing from the producer to a consumer and then to another consumer. There should be an arrow from each of these organisms to the decomposers.
  2. Are decomposers producers or consumers? Explain. Decomposers are consumers. They do not make their own food.
Activity 7.4.3 — are all decomposers microorganisms?

Look at the photograph of the fungus growing on a dead log.

  1. Is this fungus a decomposer? Yes. It is breaking down the wood in the log as it feeds on it.
  2. Is this fungus a microorganism? It is not a microorganism when it is producing toadstools. At other times, when there are no toadstools, the fungus is a microorganism — microscopic threads growing through the wood.
  3. A slug eats the fungus. Where did the slug's energy originally come from? From sunlight. The tree used energy in sunlight to make food; some of that energy passed to the fungus as it fed on the wood, and then to the slug as it fed on the fungus.
  4. Draw that food chain. tree → fungus → slug.
  5. What other microorganisms act as decomposers? Bacteria.
